papers.title: Switching from Intravenous to Subcutaneous Infliximab in Children with Inflammatory Bowel Disease: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
papers.abstract:
PURPOSE OF REVIEW: Subcutaneous infliximab (IFX-SC; CT-P13 SC/infliximab-dyyb/Remsima-SC/Zymfentra) is an approved maintenance option after intravenous (IV) induction in adults with inflammatory bowel disease (IBD), but it is not approved for patients < 18 years, and the pediatric evidence remains dispersed across small, largely observational cohorts. This review synthesizes the published pediatric experience of transitioning from IV to SC infliximab, examining maintenance of remission, drug concentrations, safety, and acceptability, and situates it within the adult evidence base and the distinctly pediatric concerns of access and dosing.
RECENT FINDINGS: A systematic search (PROSPERO: CRD420261465026) identified six independent, non-overlapping pediatric switch cohorts (n = 173). Random-effects proportional meta-analysis yielded pooled treatment persistence of 92% (95%CI 84-98), maintained clinical remission of 93% (95%CI 84-99), and any-cause discontinuation of 8% (95%CI 2-16), most often for injection-site intolerance, disease relapse, or paradoxical dermatitis. New anti-drug antibody formation was rare among the 129 children in cohorts measuring immunogenicity (four children, none sustained) while previously positive antibodies frequently resolved after switching. Steady-state SC concentrations ran roughly 2-fold above prior IV troughs, an expected step-up reflecting sustained subcutaneous exposure. Patient and caregiver satisfaction was high due to decreased school absence and travel, and cost analyses signaled net savings from avoided infusion-center use. The principal barrier was administrative: age-based denial. In appropriately selected children, transition to IFX-SC sustains remission with predictable pharmacokinetics, a reassuring immunogenicity profile, and excellent tolerability, mirroring the adult experience. These observations constitute a well-supported real-world signal and warrant prospective validation and pursuit of pediatric labeling.

papers.title: Impact of Phosphatidylinositol 3-Kinase and B-Raf Mutations in Rat Sarcoma Wild-Type Metastatic Colorectal Cancer
papers.authors: Wang W, Wang T, Qian L, Nie Y
papers.abstract: Activating mutations in phosphatidylinositol-4,5-bisphosphate 3-kinase catalytic subunit alpha (PIK3CA) and B-Raf proto-oncogene (BRAF) are hypothesized to confer primary resistance to anti-epidermal growth factor receptor (anti-EGFR) monoclonal antibodies in metastatic colorectal cancer (mCRC). However, the clinical impact of these mutations in patients with rat sarcoma (RAS) wild-type tumors remains incompletely characterized. This systematic review and meta-analysis evaluated the association of PIK3CA and BRAF mutations with clinical outcomes in RAS wild-type mCRC patients receiving first-line EGFR inhibitor therapy. A systematic literature search was conducted across PubMed, Embase, the Cochrane Library, Google Scholar, and OVID from inception through June 2019, following Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) guidelines. From 600 screened records, 10 studies comprising 1,478 patients with RAS wild-type mCRC were included. Pooled hazard ratios (HRs) for progression-free survival (PFS) and overall survival (OS), and risk differences (RDs) for objective response rate (ORR), were calculated using fixed- or random-effects models with 95% confidence intervals (CIs). PIK3CA mutations were associated with significantly worse PFS (HR, 1.38; 95% CI, 1.11-1.71; p = 0.004) and OS (HR, 1.58; 95% CI, 1.22-2.05; p < 0.001). BRAF mutations were similarly associated with worse PFS (HR, 1.68; 95% CI, 1.46-1.94; p < 0.001) and OS (HR, 1.27; 95% CI, 1.09-1.49; p = 0.003). No significant difference in ORR was observed for either PIK3CA mutations (RD, -0.12; 95% CI, -0.38 to 0.15; p = 0.38) or BRAF mutations (RD, -0.12; 95% CI, -0.28 to 0.04; p = 0.15) compared with wild-type. These findings confirm that PIK3CA and BRAF mutations are negative prognostic biomarkers in RAS wild-type mCRC, associated with inferior PFS and OS but not ORR. Incorporating BRAF and PIK3CA mutation testing into pretreatment evaluation is supported, and alternative therapeutic strategies for mutation carriers are needed. Prospective validation in larger studies is warranted.

papers.title: Fusobacterium nucleatum: a keystone bridging pathogen in polymicrobial biofilms and host immune dysregulation
papers.journal_full: Frontiers in cellular and infection microbiology
papers.authors: Sima J, Ji S, Zhang G, Li S, Sun S, Dong W
papers.abstract: Oral infectious diseases such as periodontitis stem from disrupted homeostasis between host immunity and polymicrobial biofilm communities. Fusobacterium nucleatum, a ubiquitous oral commensal, is a key intermediate colonizer with well-documented interspecies coaggregation activity. It has been proposed as a bridging pathobiont that contributes to microbial dysbiosis and immune dysregulation at the host-microbe interface, though its in vivo structural bridging function remains debated. This mini-review synthesizes recent advances in understanding the dual functions of F. nucleatum in interspecies microbial interactions and host pathogenic crosstalk. We first delineate the molecular basis of its structural bridging role, focusing on surface adhesins FadA and Fap2 that mediate interspecies coaggregation, support colonization by late-periodontopathogens such as Porphyromonas gingivalis, and enable epithelial barrier invasion. We then dissect mechanisms by which F. nucleatum modulates innate and adaptive immune responses, propagating chronic inflammatory tissue damage while subverting host clearance pathways. Furthermore, we discuss synergistic pathogenicity with co-occurring pathogens and the systemic implications of disseminated F. nucleatum in extraoral disorders including colorectal cancer and adverse pregnancy outcomes. Finally, we highlight the translational promise of targeting F. nucleatum-mediated adhesion and immunomodulation as an ecological therapeutic strategy for oral infections and their systemic sequelae.

papers.title: Patient-aware single-cell analysis of fibrovascular remodeling in a predominantly colorectal cancer immunotherapy cohort
papers.authors: Gu Y, Li L, Zhang Y, Tang J, Wang Z, Luo X
papers.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Cancer-associated fibroblasts (CAFs) and vascular mural cells may shape extracellular matrix organization in colorectal cancer. However, single-cell comparisons are susceptible to unequal cell recovery, ambient RNA, doublets, treatment-stage mixing, and repeated sampling within patients. We investigated fibrovascular remodeling using patients as the inferential unit and distinguished reproducible signals from donor-concentrated and context-dependent findings.
METHODS: We reanalyzed a published single-cell RNA sequencing cohort of 22 patients, including 20 with colorectal cancer and 2 with duodenal carcinoma. The primary pericyte analysis included 14 pretreatment matched normal-tumor pairs with at least three pericytes per tissue. We assessed ambient contamination and doublets using DecontX and scDblFinder. CAFs were reclustered at six response-blind resolutions, and the stable parent population was tested by patient-blocked pseudobulk analysis after excluding its dominant donor. Independent CRC single-cell and spatial datasets, a cross-cancer immunotherapy cohort, and TCGA were used for external testing.
RESULTS: After DecontX correction, tumor pericytes had higher ECM6 scores (median paired change 0.309; false discovery rate [FDR] 0.018). Scores were also higher for the matrix stiffness transcriptional proxy (0.277; FDR 0.012) and the hypoxia/angiogenesis transcriptional program (0.255; FDR 0.028). All three signatures remained significant at the five-pericyte threshold (n=13). COL1A1 and FN1 increased in the analysis, although COL1A1 was borderline in the five-cell sensitivity analysis. Response-blind stability analysis identified a 2,983-cell ECM-remodeling CAF population represented in all 22 patients. After excluding P02, patient-blocked pseudobulk analysis in 15 patients showed higher matrix, inflammatory, and myCAF-related programs and a lower iCAF program. Neither SPP1 nor baseline enrichment in stable disease was supported. In GSE205506, a disjoint 10-gene fibroblast gate retained higher inflammatory and composite CAF scores in non-pCR samples. The highest-scoring unsupervised cluster was donor-concentrated and showed no patient-level association with response. Spatial and cross-cancer analyses yielded mixed or null results.
CONCLUSIONS: These results support pretreatment fibrovascular transcriptional remodeling at the patient level. They do not establish an SPP1-high response biomarker, a mechanical stiffness phenotype, or causal CAF-to-pericyte signaling. Donor-aware analysis places the rare-cluster observation within a broader, reproducible ECM-remodeling CAF program while defining its evidential limits.

papers.title: International expert consensus on managing elective hernia repair in patients with Crohn's disease using the Delphi method
papers.authors: Lovén H, Helgstrand F, Friis-Andersen H, Ballecer C, Berrevoet F, Boermeester M
papers.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Patients with Crohn's disease (CD) may be predisposed to mesh-related complications such as impaired wound healing and fistula formation following hernia repair. With limited evidence and no established guidelines for hernia repair in CD, this Delphi study aimed to establish a hernia expert consensus on elective inguinal, incisional, and parastomal hernia repair in patients with CD.
METHODS: A three-round Delphi process including 21 hernia experts from Europe and the USA was conducted between 24 April and 15 October 2025. The primary outcome of interest was a consensus ≥ 75% among participants. Near consensus was defined as ≥ 70% agreement. Statements were developed from participant comments and questionnaire responses. Experts evaluated statements on timing, surgical approach, and mesh selection (synthetic non-absorbable, synthetic absorbable, biosynthetic, biological, and non-mesh) across different CD subtypes in elective inguinal, incisional, and parastomal hernia repair. Patients were categorized into three CD subtypes, namely abdominal fistulizing Crohn's disease (FCD), isolated perianal FCD, and non-FCD, with each assessed in both active and non-active inflammatory disease states.
RESULTS: Consensus or near consensus was achieved for 12 of 20 items (60%) in Round 1, 17 of 33 items (52%) in Round 2, and 13 of 29 items (45%) in Round 3. Overall, 42 of 72 unique items reached consensus (34 items) or near consensus (8 items). It was suggested that elective hernia repair should be avoided in CD patients with active inflammation, regardless of abdominal FCD or non-FCD. In non-active CD, synthetic non-absorbable mesh was suggested for inguinal, incisional, and parastomal hernia repair. Standard mesh placement was recommended for inguinal hernias, whereas retromuscular or preperitoneal mesh placement was recommended for incisional and parastomal hernias. No consensus was reached to avoid elective repair in isolated perianal FCD with active inflammation. The use of non-mesh repair, synthetic absorbable, biological, or biosynthetic mesh was generally not recommended in the elective setting.
CONCLUSIONS: Consensus was reached that CD with non-active inflammation does not require deviation from standard hernia repair principles provided that the mesh is positioned in extraperitoneal positions. However, patients with CD may have an increased perioperative risk and the surgical management should be guided by shared decision-making.

papers.title: Release and Targeting Mechanism of Nanomedicine Delivery System in Inflammatory Bowel Disease
papers.authors: Wang H, Zhou F, Shen M, Zhou S, Ma R, Yu Q
papers.abstract: Inflammatory bowel disease (IBD), encompassing Crohn's disease (CD) and ulcerative colitis (UC), arises from multifactorial pathogenesis involving colonic barrier dysfunction, gut microbiota dysbiosis, and aberrant immune regulation. The complexity of these mechanisms poses substantial challenges to achieving curative outcomes, necessitating long-term maintenance therapies. Conventional therapeutic agents (5-aminosalicylic acids, glucocorticoids, immunosuppressants, and biologics) are constrained by inherent limitations including poor solubility, chemical instability, non-specific biodistribution, and off-target toxicity, which collectively compromise therapeutic efficacy and safety. To address these challenges, nanomaterial drug delivery systems (NDDS) have emerged as a transformative strategy to enhance drug solubility, achieve spatiotemporal control, and improve intestinal targeting while reducing systemic exposure. Building upon our prior review that established a taxonomy of NDDS, this review outlines the in vivo delivery mechanisms of nanomedicine delivery systems for IBD, with the organic integration of drug-loading strategies, drug administration routes, stimulus-responsive release, and targeting mechanisms as the core framework. By systematically integrating these multidimensional mechanisms throughout the entire drug administration lifecycle, this review constructs a theoretical framework that combines macroscopic vision with mechanistic depth, laying the foundation for the rational design of next-generation intelligent NDDS and providing systematic theoretical support for improving the treatment efficacy of IBD, minimizing systemic toxicity, and promoting the clinical translation of NDDS.

papers.title: Objective validation of the Crohn's Anal Fistula Quality of Life questionnaire using quantitative MRI fistula volume in perianal fistulising Crohn's disease
papers.journal_full: Colorectal disease : the official journal of the Association of Coloproctology of Great Britain and Ireland
papers.authors: Anand E, Pelly T, Patel U, Callan R, Kanani R, Hart A
papers.abstract:
BACKGROUND: The Crohn's Anal Fistula Quality of Life (CAF-QoL) questionnaire is the first disease-specific patient-reported outcome measure (PROM) for perianal fistulising Crohn's disease (pfCD). However, validation against objective measures of disease burden is limited. We evaluated the relationship between CAF-QoL and quantitative MRI fistula volume to determine whether MRI-derived disease burden supports the construct validity of this PROM.
METHODS: Adults with pfCD were prospectively recruited from a tertiary referral centre. Patients underwent pelvic MRI and completed CAF-QoL within 3 months of imaging. MRI fistula volume was independently quantified by two radiologists using ITK-SNAP, with concurrent scoring of the Van Assche Index (VAI). Clinical disease activity was assessed using the Perianal Disease Activity Index (PDAI). Associations between MRI measures, CAF-QoL and PDAI were evaluated cross-sectionally and longitudinally.
RESULTS: Thirty-eight patients were included. MRI fistula volume correlated with both CAF-QoL (ρ = 0.40, p = 0.03) and PDAI (ρ = 0.59, p < 0.001). Patients achieving CAF-QoL remission had significantly smaller fistula volumes than those with active disease (279 vs. 965 mm3, p = 0.04). Longitudinal changes in fistula volume correlated with changes in CAF-QoL (ρ = 0.61, p = 0.02) and PDAI (ρ = 0.74, p ≤ 0.01). There was no significant association between the VAI and either CAF-QoL or PDAI. Inter-observer agreement for MRI volume measurement was excellent (ICC = 0.995).
CONCLUSION: Quantitative MRI fistula volume provides objective construct validation of the CAF-QoL questionnaire and captures clinically meaningful disease burden in pfCD. Combined assessment of MRI fistula volume and CAF-QoL may provide complementary imaging and patient-reported endpoints for clinical practice and future therapeutic trials. Larger prospective multicentre studies are warranted.

papers.title: Research trends and hotspots in colorectal cancer screening: Bibliometric and visualization analysis (2015-2024)
papers.authors: Zhou J, Zhou H, Xu J, Wang M, Liu L, Tang X
papers.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Colorectal cancer (CRC), is a highly prevalent malignant tumor worldwide, and early screening is key to improving its prognosis. Currently, CRC screening research is growing exponentially, but its core research hotspots, evolutionary trends, and interdisciplinary features are not clear. In this study, we used bibliometric analysis to analyze the distribution of literature, research hotspots, and cutting-edge developments in the field of CRC screening worldwide, and to provide a scientific basis for optimizing screening strategies.
METHODS: Publications on CRC screening from 2015 to 2024 were retrieved from the Web of Science Core Collection. VOSviewer (v1.6.20), RStudio (v4.4.1), and CiteSpace (v6.4.2) were used for bibliometric and visual analyses. The main analyses included publication trends, countries, authors, journals, references, and keywords.
RESULT: A total of 3245 publications were included in the analysis. Global publications on CRC screening showed a steady upward trend over the past decade, with an annual growth rate of 2.17%. The United States contributed the highest number of publications, and the University of North Carolina ranked as the most productive institution. GASTROENTEROLOGY and GUT were the most frequently cited journals in this field. Lansdorp‑Vogelaar I was among the most prolific authors. The most cited article was "CRC screening for average-risk adults: 2018 guideline update from the American Cancer Society." Keyword analysis showed that the research hotspots in this field included colonoscopy, biomarker, adenoma detection rate, artificial intelligence, etc.
CONCLUSION: Current research in CRC screening focuses on traditional screening methods, population-related factors, and emerging technologies, particularly artificial intelligence. Stronger international collaboration and interdisciplinary studies are needed to advance the field.
